abstract_text: We reanalyzed the data of a recently published study of higher-level snake relationships, which was based on a UPGMA analysis of alleles at four "slowly-evolving" protein-coding loci. The distance matrix derived from these data contains a large number of ties, which are not explicitly revealed in many UPGMA programs. Our analyses of these data reveal that the single, well-resolved phenogram presented in the published study is only one among at least 9,999 equivalent UPGMA phenograms supported by the data, the consensus of which is largely unresolved. Additive distance analysis and character-based parsimony analysis of the same data yield even less resolution. Thus, regardless of one's preference regarding analytical approaches, the data in question are highly ambiguous concerning higher-level snake phylogeny. The highly resolved tree presented in the published study is an analytical artifact that was obtained only because the analysis failed to consider equivalent trees resulting from ties in the distance matrix.

abstract_text: Microsatellite variation was surveyed in six populations of lean lake trout and two populations of siscowet lake trout from Lake Superior using heterologous primer pairs developed for brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) and Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). The number of alleles varied from 4 to 21 at different loci. Mendelian inheritance was confirmed for all loci. Significant differences in allele frequencies were found for lean populations from geographically distant regions and for leans and siscowets from the same regions. Genetic differences between southern and northern populations which were found in a previous study using allozyme loci were confirmed with the microsatellite loci. Comparison of our results with previous allozyme surveys and a recent study of microsatellite frequencies in lake trout hatchery stocks and populations from inland Canadian lakes suggests that there is more within lake variation in large lakes compared to small lakes and wild populations compared to hatchery stocks.

title: Stock identification of dolphin, Coryphaena hippurus, in the western central Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico and eastern Caribbean using molecular genetic techniques

authors.affiliation: University of Charleston, Grice Marine Lab, 205 F. Johnson Rd., Charleston, SC 29412

abstract_text: The dolphin, Coryphaena hippurus, is a fast swimming, migratory, pelagic fish that supports important commercial and recreational fisheries throughout the tropical and subtropical waters of the world. Oxenford and Hunte (1986) suggested two distinct stocks exist in the western central Atlantic. The southern stock migrates from Grenada northwards to the Virgin Islands and then returns southeastwards in the Atlantic. The northern stock migrates from Puerto Rico northwards to North Carolina and returns via Bermuda. The purpose of my study is to test Oxenford and Hunte's (1986) two stock hypothesis and investigate the possible presence of additional stocks using mitochondrial DNA analysis. Dolphin samples were obtained throughout their range in the western central Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean by port sampling and attending offshore fishing tournaments. Preliminary results from restriction fragment length polymorphisms of the ND-1 region of the mitochondrial genome will be reviewed. Significant genetic differences between geographic localities provides strong evidence of demographic isolation and indicates the need for independent management of individual stocks (Dixon 1992, Moritz 1994). In August 1997, the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council proposed management options for the highly migratory dolphin fishery. Data provided by this study on the stock identification of the dolphin should be beneficial to the management of this fishery throughout the western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean.

abstract_text: Basking shark populations have been subject to exploitation for many years and are currently considered to be endangered in European waters. However, little is known of their population structure. In the recent past, population structure assessments have been made on the basis of capture-mark-recapture studies or differentiation of meristic and morphological characteristics of different stocks. However, for a species such as the basking shark, which are not easy to tag in large numbers, and which little is known about their ecology, a new approach is required. Molecular genetic methods are increasingly being used with success in determining the stock structure of commercially important fish species in both marine and freshwater environments. In particular, the use of microsatellite DNA sequences is finding increasing use in fisheries stock assessment. This poster presents reports on work to develop microsatellite DNA markers for use in assessing the population structure and migratory behaviour of basking sharks in the north-east Atlantic.

abstract_text: Fundulus heteroclitus is an abundant estuarine fish found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. This species has been the subject of numerous investigations of its own biology and has been used as a tool to study xenobiotic metabolism, development, and ecology. Hybrids between Fundulus heteroclitus and F. diaphanus from Nova Scotia reproduce clonally, and thus all individuals are genetically identical. Heterozygosity at codominantly expressed enzyme loci is detectable for all enzymes for which the parental species differ, with the exception of isocitrate dehydrogenase for which the F. diaphanus is not expressed. We have amplified the cytochrome b gene from the mitochondrial genome and cut it with restriction enzymes for which the two parental species have distinct restriction patterns to determine if the lack of expression of the F. diaphanus IDH allele is due to inactivation of a paternal allele, a phenomenon occasionally observed in hybrids. The hybrids share the restriction patterns of F. diaphanus, indicating that F. diaphanus is the maternal parent of the hybrid lineage. Lack of expression of the F. diaphanus allele must therefore be due to a mutation that inactivated this allele or another rare event.

abstract_text: RAPD markers are powerful tools in the analysis of genetic relationships and genetic diversity. Recently, however, questions have risen concerning the inheritance patterns and the reproducibility of the RAPD markers. In this study, fragments generated by RAPD primers were tested for Mendelian inheritance in sailfin mollies. Mollies were collected from three locations in Florida, and over 25 single-pair matings of parents with known RAPD genotypes were made. Progeny from each mating were used to test patterns of inheritance. Of the sixty RAPD primers initially screened, 18 amplified polymorphic bands and two showed no variation. title: Evolution of germ-cell determining genes in amphibians

abstract_text: Amphibians have been widely used as model systems for studying the early embryonic development of vertebrates. Although much of the early development of all amphibians is very similar, frogs and salamanders differ strikingly in the way they determine the germ cell lineage (the cells that will form eggs and sperm). The pattern observed in frogs is quite different than the one seen in other vertebrates; the salamander mechanism is apparently much more similar to that of birds and mammals. Although the pattern of germ cell formation has been elucidated in a wide variety of species, little is known about the genes governing this process. Because most major embryological events are controlled by genes that have been highly conserved evolutionarily, it is logical to conclude that genes involved in germ cell determination will also be similar in a wide variety of species. Three genes - daz, oct-3/4 and vasa - have been shown to be critical for germ cell determination in mammals. We have used phylogenetic methods to analyze the homologous genes from frogs and salamanders to investigate whether the evolution of germ cell specific genes reflects the mode of germ cell determination (salamanders being more similar to mammals) or the phylogenetic relationships of the organisms (salamanders and frogs being more closely related). Our preliminary results suggest that germ cell determining genes from two different salamanders are more closely related to the mammalian homologues than to anuran ones, supporting the idea that the evolution of the genes tracks the mode of cell determination rather than the animal phylogeny.

abstract_text: The Waccamaw killifish (Fundulus waccamensis), a derivative of F. diaphanus, was originally thought to be endemic to Lake Waccamaw and tributaries. Recently, however, samples thought to be F. waccamensis have been collected in Lake Phelps. These samples differ morphologically from those found in Lake Waccamaw implying that they are not the product of an accidental introduction of F. waccamensis into Lake Phelps. The large geographical distance between Phelps and Waccamaw and the absence of F. waccamensis in intervening bay lakes, suggests that these populations might be remnants of a once widespread species, or, alternatively, might have arisen independently from F. diaphanus. We investigate these hypotheses using phylogenetic analyses of mtDNA control region sequences sampled from F. waccamensis (Lakes Phelps and Waccamaw) and F. diaphanus.

abstract_text: The prairie pothole region of North Dakota contains numerous wetlands of varying habitat quality. abstract_text: Lampetra aepyptera is a widespread species of non-parasitic lamprey found throughout the eastern United States. Previous studies have shown that certain populations of this lamprey exhibit heterochrony, by acheiving sexual maturity without completing metamorphosis. A preliminary survey of allozyme variation was performed to evaluate the extent of genetic differentiation among populations exhibiting either normal metamorphosis or truncated head development. The products of 22 loci were surveyed. Highly significant differentiation was observed among populations. A population from western Kentucky (Terrapin Creek) was highly differentiated from eastern Kentucky and Ohio populations, included several fixed allele differences. Because no metamorphosed adults have ever been collected from Terrapin Creek, it appears to be a new paedomorphic species. Furthermore, allele frequencies among the Terrapin Creek size classes were not different, suggesting variable time to reproduction in this population. The eastern Kentucky population (Big Sinking Creek) exhibits some evidence of incomplete metamorphosis. The presently recognized least brook lamprey appears to contain multiple species with a complex pattern of intra- and interspecific heterochrony. Additional allozyme and morphological studies are underway.

abstract_text: Reef fish assemblages are strongly influenced by reef structure. In areas where visibility is poor, specific visual census methods are necessary to determine the fish community structure. This work, part of a broader study of Brazilian reef fishes community structure, aimed to establish specific visual census methods to determine the fish community structure in rocky reefs, areas characterized by high turbidity, strong currents and irregular substrate. Five strip-transect protocols (5m depth dives) were made; 5 x 2m/intensive search without defined time, 10 x 2m/5min, 20 x 4m/5min, 40 x 4m/10min and 50 x 4m/10min. An inventory of the fishes and a comparative study of the community structure was made at Marine State Parks Laje de Santos (24° 19' S and 46° 11' W) and at Alcatrazes Archipelago (24° 06' S and 45° 42' W), off Sao Paulo State. Diversity index indicated that the transect 50 x 4m/10min is the most adequate for the studied areas, and that species number nearly stabilized at 40 x 4m/10min. 28 species were censused and protocols were produced for each one. Laje de Santos showed 19 species and Alcatrazes 21 species. Twelve censused species occurred in both areas.

title: The influence of limiting resources on growth and survival of stream-dwelling cutthroat trout

abstract_text: Two key resources are generally thought to limit salmonid populations in streams: the supply of food and the amount of suitable space within the channel. However, the relative influence of these limiting factors can change seasonally. Both food and habitat availability can affect individual fitness, but to what extent does each factor influence salmonid growth and survival on a seasonal basis? I performed a summer field experiment to directly test the effect of food and cover on growth and survival of stream-dwelling coastal cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarki clarki). Using a 2x2 factorial design, I manipulated food and cover in stream enclosures containing individually marked trout. Fish receiving food addition experienced growth rates more than 25 times higher than those of unfed fish. There was no effect of cover on either growth or survival. These results indicate that trout were severely food-limited during summer. During winter, I combined a mark-recapture study of fish with stream habitat surveys to determine the extent to which habitat complexity limits growth and survival. Finally, to address how summer growth affects over-winter survival, I monitored fish released back into the stream from the summer experiment throughout winter.

abstract_text: Spatial and temporal patterns in trophic structure of fishes from Agua Nanci creek, upper Parana river basin (Brazil) were assessed. Three monthly samples were taken from May 1996 to January 1997 using electrofishing, in three segments of the creek (near the spring, middle of its extension, and near the mouth). Food spectrum was obtained by analyzing gastric contents, with occurrence and volumetric methods, using the alimentary index. Trophic categories were established based on: the main food item, the interpretation of the Detrended Correspondence Analysis - DCA, and Average-linkage clustering (Euclidean Distance-UPGMA). The relative abundance of the food resources was estimated based on stomach content analysis. Diversity and food resources increased towards the mouth and were related to the conservation of riparian vegetation and to longitudinal hydro-morphological gradients of the creek. Temporal variations in food resources were associated with seasonal prey and hydrological cycles, thereby influencing the proportions of dominant trophic categories. Omnivores predominated in the upper part and benthivores near the mouth. Piscivores and detritivores presented low biomass. Longitudinal distribution of the trophic categories did not follow the river continuum concept, but was more related to food resources, habitat heterogeneity and the conservation conditions in each segment of the creek.

title: Impacts of Bufo boreas and Rana luteiventris tadpoles on algae and snails in ponds of Yellowstone National Park

abstract_text: Decline in frog and tadpole populations may alter trophic structures and ecosystems. During summer 1997 I investigated impacts of tadpole populations on food webs in ponds of Yellowstone National Park. The field component of this project involved two phases - experimental manipulations in enclosures and landscape-level comparison of unmanipulated ponds with and without tadpoles. In separate experiments, I stocked three blocks of enclosures with or without tadpoles of Rana luteiventris and Bufo boreas. In the experiment with Bufo boreas tadpoles, I compared their impacts with those of freshwater snails. Every two weeks until tadpole metamorphosis I measured tadpole and snail length, and collected samples of algal biomass. Results showed the Rana luteiventris tadpoles depressed algal biomass after two weeks of growth, but not after four weeks. Bufo boreas tadpoles did not depress algal biomass, but snails did. In the landscape-level project I compared eleven unmanipulated ponds, five with tadpoles and six without. This comparison did not show a statistically significant impact of tadpoles on algal biomass. Results of the two phases of this project suggest that enclosures accurately mimicked conditions in whole ponds, and that tadpole grazing had a complex influence on algal biomass, rather than a direct negative impact.

abstract_text: Low-head dams are a possible means to control spawning migration of parasitic sea lamprey, Petromyzon marinus, in tributary streams of the Laurentian Great lakes. This would reduce the need for chemical control. We studied the effects of low-head dams on stream fish communities by comparing streams with dams to paired reference streams without dams. We used electrofishing to sample streams above and below dams, and corresponding sections of barrier streams at three different seasons during the year. Fish were marked according to the location of first capture. The dams appear to block upstream movements of sea lamprey. Movements of fish above and below the locations of dams, or corresponding sites on reference streams, did not differ among streams. Upstream movements of fish over dams was reduced, compared to reference streams. The longitudinal decrease in fish species diversity from downstream to upstream sections is greater for streams with dams than for matched reference streams. Our study identified fish species most vulnerable to the effects of low-head dams and suggested likely mechanisms for this impact.

title: Microhabitat selection and social organization of overwintering juvenile coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) in a Lake Superior tributary

abstract_text: Little is known about the ecology of stream-dwelling coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) in the Lake Superior drainage. Unlike in their native range of the Pacific Northwest, Lake Superior coho salmon inhabit streams characterized by low winter flows and highly variable summer flows. Because high stream flows can profoundly influence fish behavior and distribution, we hypothesized in this study that the winter ecology of coho in Lake Superior streams would differ from patterns described for pacific populations. In snorkeling surveys completed in winter 1998, we examined the distribution and social organization of over-wintering coho in simple (no cover) and complex pools of a Lake Superior tributary in Wisconsin. In all habitats, coho occupied focal positions in the main channel; however, fish were more tightly distributed and closer to the streambanks in simple pools. Aggressive interactions also were more common in simple pools although dominance hierarchies were observed in the majority of all pools. These results are in sharp contrast with research findings from pacific streams, which generally show coho moving to protected habitats and becoming less aggressive with the onset of high flows in winter. This study provides new insights into the behavioral plasticity of coho salmon and should aid in efforts to manage Great Lake populations.

abstract_text: We assessed how biotic and abiotic factors influence the local diversity (alpha diversity) of fish communities in two rainforest streams (Itingucu e Tetequera) in the southeastern Brazil. These two streams rise in Itatins mountain, approximately at the altitude of 800 m and run into other plain rivers near the ocean. Tide influences is noticed at the lower stretches in both streams. Four sampling sites were chosen in each stream based on local physiographic features along the overall length. Fishes were collected by fykenets, dipnets, sieves and gillnets. In Tetequera 18 species were captured but only 7 were of local occurrence. The ichthyofauna of both communities showed altitudinal gradient and were formed through the processes of species addition and substitution. Species addition is more evident in the upper and medium stretches of the streams and is influence by biotic factors (vacant niche occupation and resources partitioning) and abiotic factors (physico-chemical parameters variations). On the other hand, the substitution process was more evident in the streams lower stretches as a consequence of ecological equivalence. Therefore, in these patches, abiotic factors are the main agent influencing the structure of these communities. The species diversity of each community was analyzed based on the relation between species abundance and number. The Whittaker Plot analysis of both communities suggest that they follow log series and log normal distribution.

abstract_text: The assemblage of rainforest snakes of the Manaus region, Central Amazon, was studied from 1991 to 1995. Fieldwork resulted in nearly 800 snakes of 66 forest species. Snake activity was markedly lower during the dry season. Of the 61 species for which information is available, 43% were primarily terrestrial, 31% fossorial and/or cryptozoic, 20% arboreal, and 6% aquatic. Nearly all inactive snakes were found on the vegetation. In relation to time of activity, 41% of 62 species seem to be strictly diurnal, 21% strictly nocturnal, and 38% both diurnal and nocturnal. The commonest prey were lizards (consumed by 58% of the species), frogs (39%), mammals (23%), birds (18%), and snakes (16%). A cluster analysis combining data on microhabitat use, diel activity and diet resulted in 'guilds' encompassing mostly closely related species, but also distantly related ones that converge in habits. These patterns clearly reflect the relative contribution of colubrid lineages in the assemblage, indicating that historical factors (phylogeny and biogeography) may have played and important role in determining the current organisation of this forest snake assemblage. However, current predation pressure and differential prey availability in the forest tridimensional space seem to be important in determining current patterns of microhabitat use.

abstract_text: The genus Bothrops is composed by at least five monophyletic clades. We present original data on the feeding habits of 12 species, encompassing all five clades. All species in the alternatus group seem to be mammal specialists, whose juveniles are relatively large and stout and lack pale tail tips (used to lure ectothermic prey in other species). All species of the four remaining groups are euryphagic and ontogenetic shift in prey types seems to occur in all: juveniles feed mostly on frogs and lizards, adults mainly on mammals (except for the isolated B. insularis, whose adults feed mostly on birds). Juveniles of these euryphagic species are relatively small and thin, and their tail tips are distinctly coloured (retained in adults of B. bilineatus and B. insularis). The sit-and-wait foraging tactic is the most commonly used by Bothrops, although all species may occasionally forage actively. Our results indicate that euryphagy, sit-and-wait foraging, ontogenetic shift in prey type and distinctly coloured tail tips associated with caudal luring are all plesiomorphic characters in the genus Bothrops. Mammal specialisation and the absence of distinctly coloured tail tips associated with caudal luring in juveniles may be autapomorphies of the alternatus group. (Supported by the FAPESP.)

title: Does the salt marsh snake (Nerodia clarkii) really utilize fiddler crab burrows? And how much?

abstract_text: The Nerodia clarkii complex is one that ranges from Eastern Texas, along the Gulf Coast to Volusia County, Florida. The endangered subspecies, Nerodia clarkii taeniata, and the mangrove salt marsh snake, Nerodia clarkii compressicauda, were studied to determine the percentage of snakes that were injured by the Fiddler Crab (Uca pugilator), apparently from entering the burrows. I propose that more of the behavioral ecology of Nerodia clarkii needs to be examined to understand the association of these two species.

abstract_text: Seasonal variation in sex ratio is well documented for many species of turtles, and is largely attributable to a seasonal increase in temperature. In contrast, we found a seasonal decrease in the proportion of males for Chrysemys picta even though all of the eggs were incubated at or near the pivotal temperature. This trend occured in each of the four years examined and at each of up to three sites per year. Although this trend was not always significant for the individual samples, it was significant (p = 0.005) when the years and sites were combined. If this trend were due to a minor systematic shift in incubator temperature, the lower proportions of males should have been associated with a decrease in incubation time (laying to hatching) as both incubation time and proportion of males decrease with increasing temperature. However, the sex ratio of the individual clutches was not significantly associated with incubation time in either the site or individual year samples, nor in the samples combined (p = 0.84). The slight trend for all samples combined was toward more (not fewer) males with no change in incubation times (p = 0.83). The seasonal shift in sex ratio here thus appears to be independent of temperature.

The inner ear of anurans is unique in that it contains three organs which are specialized for sound reception. The amphibian papilla (AP), the basilar papilla (BP) and the saccule (S) are anatomically distinct, spatially-separate organs each with its own complement of sensory hair cells and overlying tectorial structure. The BP and portions of the AP respond exclusively to airborne sounds whereas other portions of the AP and the S exhibit sensitivity both to airborne sounds and to substrate-borne vibrations. Measurements from the auditory periphery of Rana pipiens pipiens suggest that in contrast to BP fibers, AP fiber tuning is highly temperature-dependent. Moreover, hair cells from the rostral AP and S exhibit a clear temperature dependence in their intracellular current step response, unlike caudally-located AP and BP cells. Finally, spontaneous otoacoustic emissions, which presumably reflect hair cell motility, are highly temperature-dependent despite the fact that the upper portion of the emission frequency range (600-1600 Hz) corresponds to the domain of the BP. A model is presented that attempts to reconcile these disparate results.

title: Integrating behavior and physiology: hormones and the advertisement vocalization of male frogs

Additionally, the nightly calling has a feedback effect on the production of androgens so that vocalization itself increases androgen levels. Individual differences in nightly call effort are reflected in the variation of androgen and corticosteroid levels among calling males. Interspecific differences in call characteristics result in interspecific variation in corticosteroid levels as well.
